title: Using stitch markers
subtitle: Where to place them, when to move them, and why they save time
excerpt: Stitch markers are small clips or rings that hold a place in the work. They mark the start of a round, a key stitch, a shaping point, or an increase/decrease position. Placing them well means less counting and fewer mistakes.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book — stitch markers. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stitch marker with a clasp that closes around the yarn or the fabric of a stitch, rather than sitting on a needle tip. The standard crochet marker, since there is no needle to hold an open ring.
A stitch marker placed in the first stitch of each round to mark where the round begins. Moved to the corresponding stitch of each new round as the work progresses.

content.text: — the clasp type that clips through the fabric — rather than the open ring markers used in knitting. They clip into a stitch, not onto a needle, and travel with the work rather than sitting passively on a bar. The
is the most common use: placed in the first stitch of each round so you always know where the round begins.
Round start: clip into the first stitch of the round. Move it up to the new first stitch at the beginning of each subsequent round.
Increase/decrease positions: mark the exact stitch where shaping happens so you don't have to count from the edge every row.
Pattern repeats: place a marker every 20-30 stitches in a long row so a counting error is easy to isolate.
Armhole divide: mark the exact stitch where body and sleeve stitches separate so the division is consistent.
Clip into the stitch, not the yarn

Clip the marker through both loops of the stitch top at the position you want to mark. Not through the yarn strand itself — the marker should be free to slide out cleanly when removed. A marker clipped through a strand (rather than a stitch loop) splits the yarn when you pull it out.
What works as a marker in a pinch

A short length of contrast-colour yarn looped through the stitch and tied loosely. A safety pin (small ones, not large — large safety pins distort the stitch). A bent paper clip. The locking marker style sold specifically for crochet is convenient and cheap, but not necessary for a first project.
